hints: Focus on what you start with and what you want, a large saturated alkane going to small unsaturated propene.
Remember cracking breaks long alkanes into a shorter alkane plus an alkene, such as propene.
Ask yourself whether reduction or polymerisation makes molecules smaller and more unsaturated, or does the opposite.
walkthrough:
**Spot the goal**

Think like a refinery chemist. You have too much long-chain alkane and too little short alkene. You need to break a big molecule down and introduce a double bond.

Target product: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ (propene)

**Test cracking**

Cracking does exactly this. Heat (thermal) or heat with a catalyst (catalytic) splits a C-C bond to give a smaller alkane and a smaller alkene.

Example:
$$\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{22} \rightarrow \text{C}_{7}\text{H}_{16} + \text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}$$

**Test reduction and polymerisation**

Reduction of an organic molecule means gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen, it does not chop long alkanes into alkenes. Polymerisation joins many propene monomers together to make poly(propene), so it consumes propene instead of making it.

$$n\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6} \rightarrow \text{-[CH}_{2}\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)]}_{n}\text{-}$$

**Conclude**

Only statement 1 produces propene from larger molecules. That combination corresponds to 1 only.

options.A: Incorrect. This says 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. While cracking is correct, reduction and polymerisation do not break large alkanes down to propene.
options.B: Incorrect. This says 1 and 2 only. Cracking is correct, but reduction is not a refinery route from alkanes to alkenes, so including 2 makes this wrong.
options.C: Incorrect. This says 2 and 3 only. Both are wrong directions: reduction adds hydrogen and polymerisation joins propene up into polymer, it does not create it.
options.D: Correct. Only cracking breaks larger hydrocarbon molecules into smaller alkanes plus alkenes like propene. Reduction and polymerisation cannot do this.
